1. e4 {The king's pawn, two moves.} e5 {The same.} 2. f4 {The king's bishop's pawn, two moves.}
exf4 {The king's pawn takes the pawn.} 3. Nf3 {The king's knight, at his bishop's third square.}
g5 {The king's knight's pawn, two moves.} 4. h4 {The king's rook's pawn, two moves.} g4 {The
king's knight's pawn, one move.} 5. Ne5 {The king's knight, at the adverse king's fourth
square.} Nf6 {The king's knight, at his bishop's third square. (a) NOTE: In the former edition,
I directed the black to push the king's rook's pawn two moves. This party may be found in the
first gambit's back-game. I make two different parties of the two other ways of playing, that
were there omitted; in the first, directing the black to play the king's knight to his bishop's
third square; and in the second, to play the queen to her king's second square.} 6. d4 {The
queen's pawn, two moves. (b) NOTE: You might have taken his king's knight's pawn with your's;
but your pieces would then have been too much intangled: nevertheless, I shall make of it the
subject of a back-game.} d6 {The queen's pawn, one move.} 7. Nd3 {The king's knight, at his
queen's third square.} Nxe4 {The king's knight takes the king's pawn.} 8. Bxf4 {The queen's
bishop takes the gambit's pawn.} Qe7 {The queen, at her king's second square.} 9. Qe2 {The
queen, at her king's second square. (d) NOTE: What other piece soever he might have moved, you
should certainly have played the same, unless he had exposed some pieces to be taken.} Bg7 {The
king's bishop, at his knight's second square.} 10. c3 {The queen's bishop's pawn, one move.} h5
{The king's rook's pawn, two moves.} 11. g3 {The king's knight's pawn, one move.} d5 {The
queen's pawn, one move.} 12. Bg2 {The king's bishop, at his knight's second square.} f5 {The
king's bishop's pawn, two moves. (e) NOTE: He arms his knight with two pawns: but you must
forbear taking that piece, because by so doing you would re-unite his pawns in the centre; and
in that case his king's bishop's pawn, now useless, would get a good post, and ensure him the
game.} 13. Nd2 {The queen's knight, at his queen's second square.} Be6 {The queen's bishop, at
his king's third square.} 14. O-O {The king castles with his rook. (f) NOTE: It is better to
castle on your right than on your left side; because your king will sustain his knight's pawn,
in case he takes your queen's bishop.} Nc6 {The queen's knight, at his bishop's third square.}
15. Kh2 {The king, at his rook's second square.} O-O {The king castles. (g) NOTE: In this
position the two games are almost even. The white must make it their chief business to carry all
their forces against the adverse king's bishop's pawn, in order to take it: on the contrary, the
black ought to strive to give away the king's knight, in order to re-unite their pawns in the
centre. It is easily seen, by this gambit, that it is by no means advantageous to push the
king's rook's pawn two steps at the fourth move.} *
</script></div>

<div class="philidor-notes"><h3>Notes with no reference in the text</h3><p class="note-why">The scan lost the mark that called these, so no move points to them.</p><p><span class="note-letter">(c)</span>In the present situation he has the superiority over you of a pawn: but it is to be observed, that this pawn, which should keep the head, being left behind, will remain useless till it gets forwards to your king&#x27;s bishop&#x27;s fourth square.</p></div>
